provenance.source_title: Towards Attuned AI: Integrating Care Ethics in Large Language Model Development and Alignment

research_problem.text: How can the ethics of care inform the development and value alignment of large language models, particularly where prevailing approaches fail to account for individual vulnerability and relational context?

central_claims.text: Integrating care ethics into LLM design and value alignment offers a richer, more contextually grounded normative foundation than prevailing approaches.

evidence.text: We argue that integrating care ethics into the design and value alignment (VA) processes of LLMs offers a richer and more contextually grounded normative foundation for generative AI systems.
evidence.locator: §1.1, Introduction

evidence.text: Unlike frameworks grounded in impartiality and universality, EoC focuses on particular needs and vulnerabilities, making it particularly well-suited for LLMs deployed in domains and contexts where providing care is a fundamental aspect of the interaction, such as mental health support.
evidence.locator: §1.2, Introducing the Ethics of Care

central_claims.text: A static training-data distribution cannot adequately represent the dynamic, complex real-world settings in which LLMs operate; apparent edge cases therefore expose a consequential gap between in-distribution generalization and deployment.

evidence.text: the core issue lies in the very concept of a well-defined 'training data set distribution' being representative of the dynamic and complex real world.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

evidence.text: Human language and the world it reflects are inherently messy, with users and situations frequently existing in the 'margins' or as 'edge cases' that don't perfectly align with the training data.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.text: LLMs inherit generalization problems from feed-forward neural networks and frequently produce biased, context-insensitive, or inappropriate outputs.

evidence.text: This limitation extends directly to modern Large Language Models (LLMs), which are, at their core, massively scaled-up versions of FFNNs trained using sophisticated forms of back-propagation [Rumelhart et al., 1985]. As such, they are vulnerable to the same generalization problems.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

citations.reference_entry: David E Rumelhart, Geoffrey E Hinton, and Ronald J Williams. Learning Internal Representations by Error Propagation. 1985.

evidence.text: We see this in practice through empirical evidence that LLMs frequently exhibit representational biases and produce context-insensitive or inappropriate outputs, a problem extensively documented in recent work [Navigli et al., 2023].
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

citations.reference_entry: Roberto Navigli, Simone Conia, and Bjorn Ross. Biases in Large Language Models: Origins, Inventory, and Discussion. J. Data and Information Quality, 15(2):10:1-10:21, June 2023.

central_claims.support_assessment: The authors connect FFNN generalization limits to LLMs in §2 and cite a survey of LLM biases. That gives a rationale for concern, but the source does not itself establish that the cited biased outputs result from the particular FFNN generalization mechanism it identifies. The causal connection is less demonstrated than the existence of the two problems.

central_claims.text: Harmful biases occur across care-relevant applications, including discriminatory therapy-chatbot responses, gender-stereotyped stories, and benefit assessments that reproduce existing human biases.

evidence.text: In the realm of mental health, research has shown therapy chatbots exhibiting discriminatory responses based on users' conditions, perpetuating harmful stigmas [Harrison Dupre, 2025]. Regarding gender, LLMs have been found to generate narratives that reinforce traditional stereotypes in storytelling, demonstrating a clear gender bias in creative outputs [UCL, 2024]. Furthermore, in the context of social services, attempts to implement AI for fairer benefit assessments have resulted in the reproduction of existing human biases, highlighting the challenge of achieving equitable outcomes through purely algorithmic means [Guo et al., 2024].
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

citations.reference_entry: Maggie Harrison Dupre. Stanford Research Finds That "Therapist" Chatbots Are Encouraging Users' Schizophrenic Delusions and Suicidal Thoughts. futurism.com, June 2025.
UCL. Large Language Models generate biased content, warn researchers. ucl.ac.uk, April 2024.
Yufei Guo, Muzhe Guo, Juntao Su, Zhou Yang, Mengqiu Zhu, Hongfei Li, Mengyang Qiu, and Shuo Shuo Liu. Bias in Large Language Models: Origin, Evaluation, and Mitigation, November 2024.

central_claims.support_assessment: The three examples in §2 give the claim concrete scope, but the paper reports them through citations rather than presenting their underlying observations. In particular, the source does not explain how the cited discussion of LLM bias establishes its more specific account of benefit assessments. Their accuracy and comparability cannot be decided from this document alone.

central_claims.text: Bias in LLM outputs arises not only from training data but also from subjective values in human or AI alignment feedback.

evidence.text: This bias is not solely a product of flawed training data but also arises from the subjective values embedded in human and even AI feedback during alignment processes.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.text: Dominant frameworks emphasizing abstract utility or generalized fairness are inadequate for addressing the nuanced biases the authors identify.

evidence.text: Consequently, relying on dominant moral frameworks that prioritize abstract utility or generalized fairness proves inadequate for addressing these nuanced biases.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

evidence.text: Utilitarian approaches may justify sacrificing individual well-being for the sake of aggregated good, which is ethically troubling in contexts such as mental health or healthcare, where individual vulnerability and situational complexity demand more than mere utility maximization [Sola, 2023].
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the shortcomings of current normative commitments

citations.reference_entry: Andrew Sola. Utilitarianism and Consequentialist Ethics: Framing the Greater Good. In Ethics and Pandemics: Interdisciplinary Perspectives on COVID-19 and Future Pandemics, pages 61-83. Springer Nature Switzerland, 2023.

central_claims.support_assessment: The individual-versus-aggregate conflict in §2 explains why an aggregate criterion could miss a vulnerable person's needs. The paper does not, however, test whether existing alignment practices using fairness or utility criteria can address the particular biases it lists, or rule out combining those criteria with contextual safeguards. The reasons establish a plausible limitation, not the categorical inadequacy asserted.

central_claims.text: LLMs should be attuned to the particularities of users and their contexts rather than impose broad generalizations that may misrepresent, exclude, or harm them.

evidence.text: Instead, we should aim for systems that are attuned to the particularities of individuals and their contexts of LLM usage, rather than imposing broad generalizations that may misrepresent, exclude, or even harm them.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.text: Reorienting LLM training and design toward individual and contextual particularities, rather than statistical generalization, could mitigate harms from misapplied generalizations.

evidence.text: Re-thinking the training and design of LLMs through the lens of EoC would entail prioritizing individual and contextual particularities rather than optimizing for statistical generalization. This shift could help mitigate the harmful consequences of misapplied generalizations and align AI systems more closely with the nuanced moral demands of human interaction.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.support_assessment: The account of out-of-distribution cases and reported biases in §2 supplies a reason to attend to context. It does not show how a model could prioritize particularity instead of statistical generalization, nor demonstrate that doing so reduces the cited harms. The authors frame the benefit as a possibility, and the paper supplies a rationale for exploring it rather than an implementation or outcome test.

central_claims.text: RLHF and RLAIF embed non-neutral normative commitments: aggregated human preferences in RLHF and predefined principles or fairness criteria in RLAIF reflect utility-maximizing or justice-based approaches.

evidence.text: Current Value Alignment (VA) methods, particularly Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and its more recent variant Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF), are grounded in specific normative frameworks, primarily utilitarianism and justice-based theories such as Contractualism and Rawlsian justice. These approaches optimize behaviour either by aggregating human preferences (in RLHF), or by aligning model outputs with predefined fairness metrics or constitutional principles (in RLAIF), thus reflecting a commitment to maximizing overall utility or ensuring procedural fairness [Sola, 2023].
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the shortcomings of current normative commitments

citations.reference_entry: Andrew Sola. Utilitarianism and Consequentialist Ethics: Framing the Greater Good. In Ethics and Pandemics: Interdisciplinary Perspectives on COVID-19 and Future Pandemics, pages 61-83. Springer Nature Switzerland, 2023.

central_claims.support_assessment: The paper describes reward optimization and, later in §2, a constitutional-AI example. These illuminate particular choices, but do not establish that RLHF and RLAIF generally have the specific philosophical commitments attributed to them. A reward signal can be optimized without the source showing that its underlying moral criterion is aggregate utility; the broad characterization remains insufficiently substantiated here.

central_claims.text: In care-relevant settings, current value-alignment frameworks based on rules and aggregation prove inadequate because individual needs are emotionally laden, unique, and context-dependent.

evidence.text: Examples include healthcare, education, eldercare, and mental health support, these fields in which the needs of individuals are unique, emotionally laden, and highly context-dependent [Beauchamp, 2006]. In such settings, the current VA frameworks, grounded in rule-following and aggregation, prove inadequate.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the shortcomings of current normative commitments

citations.reference_entry: Tom L. Beauchamp. The 'Four Principles' Approach to Health Care Ethics. In Principles of Health Care Ethics, pages 3-10. Wiley, 2006.

evidence.text: Likewise, justice-based approaches may overemphasize principles such as truthfulness or impartiality, and fail to account for the emotional, relational, and context-sensitive needs of individuals in morally complex or care-relevant situations [Gilligan, 1993].
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the shortcomings of current normative commitments

citations.reference_entry: Carol Gilligan. In a Different Voice: Psychological Theory and Women's Development. Harvard University Press, 1993.

central_claims.support_assessment: The discussion of potentially conflicting priorities and context-dependent needs in §2 explains why rule- or aggregate-based responses may be insufficient. It does not establish that current frameworks cannot accommodate contextual distinctions or that they prove inadequate across the listed domains. The asserted breadth exceeds the cases and reasoning developed in the source.

central_claims.text: Anthropic's Constitutional AI declares duty-like commitments but, in the authors' account, its reward-maximizing implementation operates on utilitarian principles.

evidence.text: At this stage, an AI preference model trained to align with the constitution provides reward signals, and the system is optimized to maximize these signals [Bai et al., 2022].
evidence.locator: §2, Constitutional AI discussion

citations.reference_entry: Yuntao Bai et al. Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback, December 2022.

evidence.text: Thus, Anthropic's framework presents a deontological front, but its mechanics operate on utilitarian principles.
evidence.locator: §2, Constitutional AI discussion

central_claims.support_assessment: The reward-model description in §2 supports the narrower claim that training optimizes a score. It does not by itself show that the score represents aggregate welfare or that using optimization makes the ethical framework utilitarian. That further identification is needed for the authors' contrast between a deontological front and utilitarian mechanics.

central_claims.text: The technical implementation of Anthropic's ostensibly deontological alignment approach could only be utilitarian.

evidence.text: As we have seen, although in principle, Anthropic adopted a deontological approach to value alignment, the technical implementation could only be utilitarian.
evidence.locator: §2, end of argument from the shortcomings of current normative commitments

evidence.text: After a supervised fine-tuning phase in which the model critiques its own responses using the constitution as a reference, the training process transitions to reinforcement learning.
evidence.locator: §2, Constitutional AI discussion

central_claims.support_assessment: The paper describes a supervised critique phase followed by reinforcement learning and reward optimization in §2. That sequence does not establish the stronger 'could only' claim: no reason is given why technical implementations of the stated commitments must be utilitarian, or why the described supervised phase cannot retain a distinct role. The source supports a characterization of its chosen example, not technical inevitability.

central_claims.text: Care-informed feedback for a mental-health chatbot should weigh a user's emotional state, relational cues, and expressed needs; when a distressed user expresses suicidal thoughts, it might prioritize empathy, safety, and relational responsibility over truthfulness.

evidence.text: However, a care ethics-informed chatbot would go further by weighing feedback according to the user's current unique emotional state, relational cues, and expressed needs. A distressed user expressing suicidal thoughts might receive an AI response that prioritizes empathy, the user's safety, and relational responsibility over truthfulness.
evidence.locator: §2, mental-health-chatbot example

evidence.text: Rather than reinforcing a response simply because it is rated highly in general by annotators, the model would be trained to identify morally salient features such as signs of vulnerability, dependency, or self-harm in this particular interaction and then be allowed to adjust its behaviour accordingly.
evidence.locator: §2, mental-health-chatbot example

central_claims.support_assessment: The example makes the proposed tradeoff explicit, but does not specify what setting truthfulness aside would permit, or how empathy and safety would be assessed when they conflict with accuracy. The concluding discussion also says that models' recognition of emotional and social cues remains technically underdeveloped. This is a concrete design illustration, not evidence that the suggested priority will safely improve responses.

central_claims.text: A value-alignment method tailored to care-relevant domains and inspired by care ethics is necessary.

evidence.text: Therefore, we argue that it is necessary to develop a value alignment method tailored to care-relevant domains and contexts inspired by the ethics of care.
evidence.locator: §2, end of argument from the shortcomings of current normative commitments

evidence.text: These instances demonstrate how LLMs, despite their technical sophistication, can inadvertently entrench societal inequities in care-relevant applications.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

evidence.text: Abstract, generalized principles, or the pursuit of aggregated preference maximization, often fail to adequately address the specific vulnerabilities, individual needs, and contextual particularities inherent in these domains.
evidence.locator: §2, Constitutional AI discussion

central_claims.support_assessment: The reported harms and the argument that abstract principles can overlook particular needs (§2) support developing a context-sensitive approach. Necessity is stronger: the paper neither surveys the available alternatives exhaustively nor establishes that care-inspired alignment is required to address the harms rather than one possible route. The inferred assumption that no alternative approach could adequately meet those needs is needed for this claim.

central_claims.text: Existing techniques, including RLHF and RLAIF, can be modified to incorporate care-based principles, although the paper does not provide a full technical methodology.

evidence.text: When it comes to the technical implementation of this VA method, current methods such as RLHF and RLAIF can be modified to incorporate care-based principles. However, the comprehensive elaboration of the full technical methodology is beyond the scope of this paper. More research still needs to be done.
evidence.locator: §2, end of argument from the shortcomings of current normative commitments

central_claims.text: Care ethics should also shape human labeling by prompting labelers to consider the relational effects of responses, especially for marginalized or care-dependent populations.

evidence.text: It would also inform the work of human labelers, encouraging them to reflect not only on individual preferences, but on the broader relational impacts of AI responses, especially for marginalized or care-dependent populations.
evidence.locator: §3, Conclusion

central_claims.text: Care ethics could enrich constitutional alignment by promoting the well-being of both caregivers and care-receivers within interdependent social networks.

evidence.text: Constitutionally, care ethics could provide a richer moral foundation by promoting the well-being of both caregivers and care-receivers within interdependent social networks.
evidence.locator: §3, Conclusion

central_claims.text: Embedding a care-based moral orientation would make LLM chatbots more likely to resist sycophancy, minimize hallucinations, and engage users with greater responsibility and trust.

evidence.text: By embedding this moral orientation, LLM's chatbots would be more likely to resist sycophantic behaviour, minimize hallucinations, and engage users with a deeper sense of responsibility and trust.
evidence.locator: §3, Conclusion

central_claims.support_assessment: This predicts several distinct improvements from embedding care ethics. Earlier sections explain why attention to vulnerability could affect the appropriateness of a response, but provide no mechanism or results connecting care-informed alignment to reduced hallucinations or sycophancy. The prediction is asserted in the conclusion, and the source does not supply enough to assess its likely magnitude or reliability.

central_claims.text: Care ethics better reflects how people want to be treated in morally significant interactions with AI.

evidence.text: By offering a context-sensitive and relationally grounded framework, care ethics better reflects how people actually want to be treated in morally significant interactions with AI.
evidence.locator: §3, Conclusion

central_claims.support_assessment: The discussions of relational moral reasoning in §§1.2 and 2 explain why the authors favor this framework. They do not present evidence of how people actually want AI to treat them, including whether preferences differ across users or situations. The comparative claim about people's wants remains untested in the source.

methodology.summary: A conceptual and normative argument combining care-ethics theory, an account of LLM generalization, cited examples of bias, and analysis of RLHF, RLAIF, and Constitutional AI. A hypothetical mental-health-chatbot interaction illustrates a possible change to feedback and response priorities; no care-informed system is implemented or evaluated.
methodology.study_design: Conceptual argument and illustrative case analysis
data_sources: Care-ethics and moral-philosophy literature cited in the paper
Cited discussions of neural-network generalization and LLM bias
Descriptions of existing value-alignment methods and Constitutional AI
methodology.sample_or_scope: LLM development and alignment, particularly mental health, healthcare, education, eldercare, and social services
analysis_methods: Normative comparison of care ethics with utility- and justice-oriented approaches
Argument from generalization limits and reported application harms
Interpretation of reward optimization and constitutional alignment

assumptions.text: For the claim that a care-inspired alignment method is necessary, no other available approach could adequately address the relevant individual and relational needs in care-sensitive domains.

For the proposed feedback modification, signs of vulnerability, dependency, and emotional state can be identified and represented in training in a way that reliably improves decisions for the particular user.
For the conclusion's prediction about hallucinations and sycophancy, making a chatbot more responsive to relational context also reduces those failure modes.

limitations.text: Care ethics resists formalization and scalability, and its limited procedural structure may hinder transparency and consistency in automated systems.
The paper does not develop the full technical methodology for a care-inspired value-alignment method.

Current models lack genuine understanding of vulnerability, dependency, and relational dynamics, while the ability to recognize and respond to complex emotional and social cues remains technically underdeveloped.
The paper provides no implementation or evaluation of whether care-informed alignment reduces the harms or failure modes it identifies.

proposed_solutions.text: Develop a value-alignment method for care-relevant domains that incorporates care ethics and prioritizes responsiveness to individual vulnerabilities and relational context.
Modify RLHF or RLAIF feedback and reinforcement so that models attend to morally salient features of particular interactions rather than relying only on generally high-rated responses.
Incorporate consideration of broader relational impacts into human labeling and use care ethics to inform constitutional principles concerning caregivers and care-receivers.
Pursue further interdisciplinary research and cautious implementation when bringing care ethics into AI design.

open_questions.text: How can contextual and relational care principles be translated into transparent, consistent alignment procedures without losing the attention to particularity that motivates them?
How can an LLM reliably recognize vulnerability and emotional or relational cues, and resolve conflicts among empathy, safety, and truthfulness in an individual interaction?
Would a care-informed alignment method reduce bias, sycophancy, or hallucinations in deployed systems, and how should those outcomes be evaluated?
